# 

# Psychedelics and prevention: A research roadmap to expanded access and improved population health

# Abstract

**Background:** Psychedelic-assisted interventions show promise for reducing problematic substance use, major contributors to preventable morbidity and mortality. While psychedelic research has largely adopted a treatment framework, a complementary prevention framework could intervene earlier in behavioral and disease trajectories, increasing population health impact, cost-effectiveness, and access. We applied a prevention framework to psychedelic interventions to develop a research roadmap toward U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) evidentiary standards for tobacco, alcohol, and opioid use; meeting those standards could trigger insurance coverage for psychedelic preventive care without cost-sharing.

**Methods:** We evaluated 42 eligible clinical-trial publications addressing alcohol (n=32), opioids (n=6), and tobacco (n=4) against USPSTF criteria, examining methodological design, population and generalizability, intervention and safety, equity, outcomes, and follow-up; 33 observational studies were also reviewed. Net benefits were assessed, and the evidence was benchmarked against analogous USPSTF Grade A/B preventive interventions.

**Results:** Psychedelic trials generally demonstrated external validity limitations. Only 2% addressed primary care settings or populations; representation of women and racially/ethnically diverse populations was limited; and implementation outcomes, quality of life, and equity were infrequently assessed. Nonetheless, 81% of trials reported improvement in problematic substance use, with a pooled effect size of 2.30 (1.49–3.55). Among the 86% assessing adverse events (AEs), 28% recorded at least one moderate/severe AE; severe events constituted 13% of 185 recorded AEs, while 78% were mild. Benchmarking suggests that developing an evidence base meeting USPSTF standards may be feasible.

**Recommendations:** A prevention-oriented psychedelic research roadmap should prioritize external validity and primary care populations, track longer-term health outcomes, incorporate large observational and state-program data, and consider expanded access through the USPSTF. Although evidentiary gaps remain, a prevention framework could position psychedelic research to inform preventive-service policy, expand access, and improve population health.

Shorter abstract

**Background:** Psychedelic-assisted interventions show promise for reducing problematic tobacco, alcohol, and opioid use, major contributors to preventable morbidity and mortality. While research has largely adopted a treatment framework, a complementary prevention framework could intervene earlier in behavioral and disease trajectories, potentially increasing population health impact, cost-effectiveness, and access. We apply a prevention framework and develop a research roadmap toward U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) evidentiary standards; meeting those standards could trigger insurance coverage for psychedelic care without cost-sharing.

**Methods:** We evaluated 42 eligible clinical-trial publications addressing alcohol (n=32), opioids (n=6), and tobacco (n=4) against USPSTF criteria for design, generalizability, intervention and safety, equity, outcomes, and follow-up; 33 observational studies were also reviewed. Net benefits were assessed and evidence benchmarked against analogous USPSTF Grade A/B interventions.

**Results:** Trials demonstrated external validity limitations: only 2% addressed primary care settings or populations; representation of women and racially/ethnically diverse populations was limited; and implementation, quality-of-life, and equity outcomes were infrequently assessed. Net benefits were positive, with 81% reporting improvement (pooled effect size of 2.30 (1.49–3.55)). Among 86% assessing adverse events (AEs), 28% recorded at least one moderate/severe AE; severe events constituted 13% of 185 AEs, while 78% were mild. Benchmarking suggests meeting USPSTF standards may be feasible.

**Recommendations:** Research that prioritizes preventive applications, external validity, primary care populations, longer-term outcomes, observational and state-program data, and policy access pathways could help psychedelic research inform policy that expands access and improves population health.

# Introduction

## Background

Problematic substance use represents a substantial portion of the global disease burden, posing major challenges for health systems worldwide (Degenhardt et al., 2018; Whiteford et al., 2013). Despite considerable public and private investment in prevention and treatment, substance-related problems continue to represent a major public health challenge (Barbosa et al., 2018). Within this context, tobacco, alcohol, and opioids remain leading causes of preventable mortality (CDC, 2024a, 2024b; Gomes et al., 2018; GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2019 Tobacco Collaborators, 2021; Fang et al., 2025; Whiteford et al., 2013). This ongoing burden may partially reflect the limited long-term effectiveness of existing treatments for these behaviors. For example, 6-month abstinence rates for the most widely used smoking cessation pharmacotherapies range from 17.6% to 27.6% (Cahill et al., 2014). 

Even as greater study is needed (Weleff, et al., 2025), psychedelic treatments are demonstrating promise as responses to this crisis (Richard & Garcia-Romeu, 2025, Carhart-Harris & Goodwin, 2017; Nutt et al., 2020; Reiff et al., 2020). (See Table 2 for a list of substances included for this study) For example, there is emergent evidence of psychedelics’ efficacy for smoking cessation, including a recent randomized clinical trial found that those receiving psilocybin demonstrated six-fold greater odds of prolonged smoking abstinence at 6-months follow-up compared to those receiving a nicotine patch (95%CI:1.99-23.26) (Johnson, 2026; Johnson et al., 2022; Johnson et al., 2017; Glenn et al., 2025). Problematic alcohol use (AUD) may also be responsive (Andersen et al., 2021; Garcia-Romeu, et al., 2019); early trials indicate that psychedelic intervention involving psilocybin may reduce heavy drinking and daily drinking (Bogenschutz, 2022), and Sessa (2021) found MDMA- assisted psychotherapy to be safe and tolerable for patients with alcohol use disorder, contributing to reduced drinking as well. A scoping review found that in the majority of 40 studies addressing OUD, ibogaine, select derivatives and metabolites, and ketamine, could reduce opioid use, alleviate withdrawal symptoms, and change conditioned place preference (Pulido-Saavedra, et al., 2025). Pertaining to stimulants (another significant public health challenge), a psilocybin intervention was associated with 18-fold greater odds (95% CI:1.92-2468.17; P = .007) of total abstinence at 6 months than active placebo; a striking study also in that 82% of participants were Black and 65% low income  (Hendricks et. al. 2026).

Observational studies reinforce these trial findings. In a prospective cohort study of community-referred people who use drugs, psychedelic use was associated with decreased odds of subsequent daily opioid use (AOR=0.45; 95%CI: 0.29 to 0.70) (Argento, 2021). A large cross-sectional online survey found that those with at least one lifetime psychedelic experience reported that the experience improved their health behaviors, including related to alcohol (66%) and tobacco (49%) and opioid use (40%); individuals engaging in more frequent use were more likely to report positive behavioral changes (Teixeira et al., 2025). 

In a prospective, IRB-approved, real-world interventional pilot study (n=20) in Oregon, administering two psilocybin sessions (one individual and one group), along with preparation and integration sessions, to participants struggling with alcohol use led to significantly less alcohol consumption and binge drinking days as well as significantly longer periods of abstinence.  It also led to significant improvements in mental health and a significant decrease in problems related to alcohol (Grant et al., 2026). 

## Preventive Care Meets Policy Gap

Despite promising findings around efficacy, even if approved by the United States Food & Drug Administration (USFDA), implementation and economic models require further development (Marseille, Bertozzi & Kahn, 2022\) to guide their safe, scalable, and equitable integration into a fragmented U.S. healthcare system (Aday et al., 2023; Belouin et al., 2022; Marks & Cohen, 2021). Discourse regarding insurance coverage and payment feasibility is ongoing, with calls for Medicare reimbursement pathways to address cost-effectiveness (CHCS, 2026; Propes et al., 2025; Marseille, Bertozzi & Kahn, 2022).

The epistemic frame shaping these deliberations will carry policy and access implications. The current focus of psychedelic science and interventions is generally on treatment of problematic behaviors that have already progressed to later stages. The subsequent narrowing of the scope of psychedelic service implementation, access, cost coverage and reimbursement limits the potential role of psychedelics in population health. A complementary public health frame places less emphasis on treating a problematic behavior and more on preventing the adverse health outcomes associated with that behavior. While similar to a therapeutic frame in many regards, a prevention approach is nevertheless distinct as it expands the window for psychedelic interventions to earlier in behavior, health, and disease processes. Earlier, intervention is known to improve population health outcomes and reduce healthcare costs (Chen 2018; Masters, 2017; Musich, 2016; Maciosek et al., 2010). This phenomenon implies that recent studies finding  psychedelic assisted treatment to be cost effective (Avanceña, 2025; Ziadi, 2026\) would produce even greater social and economic benefits were the intervention to occur prior to development of advanced mental health conditions.

Additionally, locating psychedelic interventions within a prevention framework may also expand equitable access. In the U.S., for example, Section 2713 of the U.S. Affordable Care Act (ACA) requires that private insurers cover certain recommended primary care preventive services without cost sharing (Koh & Sebelius, 2010). 

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) is the body charged with issuing these preventive services recommendations, which have included screening for colorectal cancer, cervical cancer, breast cancer, prediabetes, and Type 2 diabetes. They also issue pharmacological preventive measures for disease prevention, including statins for cardiovascular disease, Preexposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV, tamoxifen for breast cancer risk reduction and for behavior modification, such as bupropion, varenicline, and nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation \[USPSTF\], 2021a). 

The USPSTF bases its recommendations largely on assessment of the sufficiency of the evidence in terms of the certainty and magnitude of net benefits (benefits minus harms) (Fox & Shaw, 2015). A USPSTF recommendation of grade “A” (high certainty of substantial net benefit) or “B” (high certainty of moderate net benefit or moderate certainty of moderate or substantial net benefit) for a primary care-based prevention intervention for asymptomatic people can lead to insurance coverage without cost sharing (Fox & Shaw, 2015). Although the USPSTF role has been challenged (see, for example, Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, Inc., 2025), the USPSTF currently still has a role in shaping access to preventive care that benefits millions. 

Even with supportive guidance from USPSTF, it remains a public health imperative to better understand the prevention potential of psychedelic interventions for, since current recommendations are insufficient. USPSTF-recommended pharmacotherapies for smoking cessation achieve only a 17.6–27.6% six-month abstinence (Cahill et al., 2014), limiting their ability to singularly shift population health. With regards to either alcohol or opioid use disorders, the USPSTF currently makes no pharmacotherapy recommendations: the current Grade B recommendation for unhealthy alcohol use in adolescents and adults is limited to screening and brief behavioral counseling (USPSTF, 2018; 2025), and the 2020 Grade B recommendation for screening unhealthy drug use in adults explicitly notes that screen-detected populations show no benefit from brief counseling and that evidence for pharmacotherapy benefit is restricted to treatment-seeking populations (Krist et al., 2020). USPSTF does acknowledge the benefit and role of FDA-approved pharmacotherapies (naltrexone, methadone, buprenorphine) for opioid use disorder, but ultimately, there are no pharmacological preventive options assured of insurance coverage for two of the most lethal substance use conditions in adults (Degenhardt et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2025). 

Should the science concerning preventive psychedelic-assisted intervention continue to demonstrate effectiveness and be incorporated into the primary care setting, then psychedelics could fill a significant gap in preventive care and accessibility. Further, psychedelics appear to produce concurrent improvements in depression, anxiety, well-being, and alcohol co-consumption (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2019; Raison et al., 2022; Teixeira et al., 2025). Although USPSTF's appraisal methodology evaluates each intervention independently, these co-benefits broaden the case for psychedelic-assisted prevention to produce population-level health impacts.

However, to our knowledge, psychedelic science has not incorporated a prevention frame in production of its evidence base, even as there are signs that the USPSTF may at some juncture turn their attention to psychedelics: The USPSTF’s draft Contextual Questions section of the *Research Plan for Tobacco Cessation in Adults: Interventions,* considered psilocybin (USPSTF, 2025), suggesting an emerging recognition and policy opportunity. 

The aims of this study are therefore to introduce how a public health prevention frame can apply to psychedelic interventions, highlighting population health implications and potential mechanisms of action. It then aims to set a research roadmap to meet USPSTF evidentiary standards and thereby open a policy window to expand access and population benefits. Our specific objectives are to evaluate the current body of psychedelic evidence relative to USPSTF criteria for its A or B rating and inform future research to better meet these standards for greater and more equitable regulated access.  

# Psychedelics in the context of prevention 

Figure 1 provides a schematic of how a preventive approach extends the window of intervention to earlier in the behavioral and disease trajectory. In this framework, psychedelic  interventions function not just as behavioral health treatments, but as primary or secondary prevention modifiers of morbidity, and mortality, making them eligible for consideration by the USPSTF. While this diagram is presented in the context of substance use, it could apply to other situations such as prevention of the adverse health outcomes of other known high-risk conditions such as trauma, high ACE scores, etc.

#### Figure 1: A schematic of psychedelic intervention as prevention for substance use-related adverse health outcomes

![][image1]

In a study exploring psychedelics’ preventive potential, addiction professionals agreed that psychedelics could function as preventive interventions rather than exclusively as treatment modalities (Lill, 2025). Clinical and observational data suggest psychedelics may be effective interventions for the primary and secondary prevention of adverse health outcomes linked to problematic smoking, alcohol, and opioid use. Bogenschutz (2022) found that psilocybin intervention was associated with decreased levels of the World Health Organization’s risk levels for alcohol, including improving blood pressure, the number one preventable risk factor for death worldwide. In individuals who use opioids, psychedelic use has been associated with a reduction in suicide risk among people who report at least one lifetime use of psychedelics and among individuals who use opioids (Teixeira, 2025; Argento et al., 2022), with Qeadan (2025) finding psychedelic use associated with fewer overdoses, relapses, mental health crises, and SUD-related hospitalizations or emergency department visits among people who use substances. Psychedelic use may also be associated with positive health outcomes among individuals with chronic pain, a condition that frequently co-occurs with and may contribute to problematic substance use; among adults using psychedelics to self-treat chronic pain, 78.8% reported improvements in physical health conditions, while 86.3% reported decreasing or ceasing use of at least one non-psychedelic substance, including 64.1% of those who had used prescription opioids (Glynos et al., 2025). These findings suggest that the potential preventive benefits of psychedelic interventions may extend to adverse health outcomes associated with problematic substance use. Table 1 summarizes the spectrum of the prevention window for psychedelic interventions and the potentially prevented negative health outcomes.

Psychedelic-assisted interventions may function in this preventive capacity by altering the trajectory from problematic behavior to health outcomes (Neuhaus & Slavich, 2022). Physiologically, psychedelic interventions have been linked to reduced drug cravings, which can be critical to achieving cessation (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2025; Chapron et al., 2025). Preventive psychedelic interventions may also enhance flexibility and fluidity of cognition and thought patterns (Gattuso et al., 2022), loosening the influence of deeply held beliefs that guide behavior (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019). They also seem to enhance neuroplasticity and openness to change, which in turn support the disruption of entrenched patterns of psychological and behavioral rigidity necessary for sustained behavior modification and improved health outcomes (Neuhaus & Slavich, 2022; Nardou et al., 2023; Woodburn & Kwan, 2023).

At a population health level, psychedelic practices point to net benefits that are an important consideration in preventive care. Neither lifetime nor past use of psychedelics was associated with worse mental health status than seen among the general population, and in fact for many psychedelic substances it was associated with better (Krebs, 2013). A series of studies similarly found better health, substance use, lifestyle, and well-being status among those with routine intentional ayahuasca practices compared to the general population (Ona, 2019; Kohek, 2023; Teixeira, 2026).  

From a prevention science framework, these mechanisms suggest that the potential role for psychedelics to address tobacco, alcohol, and opioid use may especially align with primary and “indicated” (targets individuals with early signs or subclinical symptoms of a disorder, but do not yet meet full diagnostic criteria) prevention approaches that alter the trajectory of disorder onset and perhaps even prevent initiation, and psychedelic intervention could be effectively partnered with a screening protocol. Even if it is early to draw definitive conclusions from psychedelic science (Mackey, 2022), it is not too early for the frame of psychedelic scholarship to include prevention. 

# Methods

This study employs a “policy backward” framework to assess the requirements for a forward-facing research roadmap to psychedelics as preventive care, with a focus on the USPSTF. The methodology is divided into three distinct parts to bridge the gap between current clinical evidence and federal prevention policy: 1\) Narrative literature review and evidence characterization, 2\) Data preparation, and 3\) Comparison with USPSTF methodological standards, screening/net benefit framework, and Category A/B benchmarks.

## Part 1: Narrative Literature Review and Characterization

The existing body of psychedelic research across tobacco, alcohol, and opioid domains was searched by drawing from data sources including PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and AI-assisted search databases. Search queries include combinations of keywords referencing “psychedelics” and its constituents (e.g., psilocybin, LSD, ibogaine) as well as substance-related keywords, e.g., tobacco, smoking, alcohol, drinking, AUD, opioid, opiate, heroin, OUD. We included clinical trials and observational studies that investigated the effects (or associations) of psychedelics with respect to substance use, craving, or recovery in human participants. While the USPSTF generally relies upon pooled studies, for our methodology we did not include pooled studies, only their constituent individual studies. 

## Part 2: Data Preparation

To evaluate the existing evidence for psychedelic-assisted therapies against USPSTF standards for Category A/B recommendations, we first reviewed the US Preventive Services Task Force Procedure Manual to identify their evidentiary standards and priorities. Subsequently, we created a codebook of 52 indicators across six domains: (1) Study Identification & Design (e.g., randomization, blinding, sample size, and validated measures); (2) Population & Generalizability (e.g., demographics and geographic settings); (3) Intervention & Safety (e.g., intervention delivery and adverse events); (4) Equity & Cultural Framing (e.g., Indigenous knowledge and community reciprocity); (5) Outcomes & Follow-Up (e.g., effect sizes and long-term behavioral endpoints. A sixth category, Substances, portrayed the distribution of research by specific substances used. While the indicators were developed for clinical trial standards, a subset also were measured for observational studies as part of the net benefit assessment (substances, safety and efficacy).

### 2.1 Extraction procedure

Each included article was coded according to these indicators through a structured, AI-augmented two-step protocol. As a first test, the full text of each article was submitted to Anthropic’s Claude Opus large language model using a fixed system prompt that instructed the model to function as an expert systematic reviewer with specialization in psychedelic science, substance-use disorders, and clinical-trial methodology. The model was required to return coded values exclusively as a single JSON object, organized according to the codebook’s variable order and response-type specifications. Second, selected outputs were reviewed and, when necessary, corrected by at least one of three human reviewers with formal training in epidemiology. Coding uncertainties and discrepancies were resolved through consensus-based discussion among the reviewer team.

Afterwards, we did a second pass of the same clinical data. Through this pass we confirmed the stability of the coding process. Each included article was coded according to the indicators through a structured, AI-augmented protocol with a deterministic validation gate. Each article's source PDF was first converted to Markdown by a fixed preprocessing script, subject to a four-check fidelity gate (text-retention ratio, runaway-expansion ratio, heading recovery, and table-row recovery); files failing any check were demoted to plain text, and optical character recognition was applied at 300 dpi where a scan yielded no usable text. Each article was assigned to an isolated Claude Sonnet 5 subagent that saw only that article, preventing cross-article contamination, in particular, preventing the methodological or demographic profile of one study from anchoring the coding of another. Each subagent returned a single JSON object containing both the coded values and a mandatory free-text rationale for every non-obvious decision. Extraction was performed under a pinned prompt version (v1.2) and a pinned severity rubric (v1), both recorded per article so that any value can be traced to the exact instructions that produced it. Severity was coded on a fixed three-level scale, mild, moderate, or severe, adapted from the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0 and FDA seriousness criteria. The scale was modified to ensure that effects expected in the context of psychedelic-assisted therapy, such as transient anxiety or perceptual distortion, were not automatically classified as more severe than warranted.

Observational studies, including cohort studies, case series, case reports, and cross-sectional designs without a concurrent comparator arm, were assessed using a narrower, purpose-built codebook limited to adverse events, challenging experiences, main effects, and basic demographic characteristics. The resulting observational-study dataset was maintained as a standalone dataset and analyzed separately from, rather than merged with, the primary clinical-trial dataset. 

### 2.2 Data cleaning, harmonization, and missing-data handling

Binary variables were coded on a four-level scheme: 1 (yes/present), 0 (no/absent), 3 (not applicable), and missing (not reported). In accordance with the USPSTF interpretive convention, missing and non-applicable values were treated as not met when quantifying the proportion of studies satisfying each indicator; this yields a conservative gap estimate that does not credit studies for unreported methodology. The raw data was processed through a Python pipeline to ensure consistency across the datasets, which included data extraction, categorization, and organization.

Each article was first screened against three eligibility criteria: (a) that it reported an original clinical trial rather than a protocol, review, or commentary, (b) that it reported at least one substance-use outcome and (c) that the outcome concerned tobacco, alcohol, or opioid use, the three conditions under review. Articles failing either criterion were retained in the dataset with an explicit failure code and reason, but excluded from all analyses. Of 49 articles screened in the clinical trial data, 42 were eligible; the 7 exclusions comprised two study protocols (O'Donnell 2022; Vanderijst 2024), two narrative reviews or methodological critiques of prior trials (Costello 1969; Smart 1964), one article reporting no substance-use outcome (Denson 1970), one article whose only available scan did not contain the target text (Ludwig 1969\) and one double-blind trial conducted entirely in cocaine-dependent patients, outside the review's three conditions (Prior 2014). Following extraction, every field on which the automated extraction disagreed with the prior extraction was independently re-adjudicated against the source text by reviewers, who recorded a decision and a written justification for each. Of 281 adjudicated fields, the automated value was upheld in 144 (51%), the prior value in 74 (26%), 34 (12%) were judged equivalent notations of the same fact, and 29 (10%) were judged unresolvable from the source text. All fields decided in favour of the hand extraction were written back into the analytic dataset. Thirtynine observational articles entered the screen. Guardrails screening for outcome flagged 10 observational as possibly not corresponding to this study’s measures. Two human reviewers subsequently removed 6 observational studies, leaving a total of 33 observational studies. 

Quality control for AE classifications involved two reviewers independently reviewing a random subsample of AI-generated AE classification reports (i.e., singular or grouped incidents of the same severity) from the clinical (23% of 194 reports) and observational publications (13% of 103 reports). Of these, 98% (44) of clinical and 92% (12) of observational AEs were correctly classified.  

## Part 3: Comparison with USPSTF methodological standards, net benefits, screening framework, and Grade A/B benchmarks

### 3.1 Methodological evaluation

To portray the certainty of evidence standard that USPSTF uses for decision-making, descriptive statistics were conducted in Python to characterize the extent to which the resulting dataset aligns with the evidentiary standards of prevention science across five domains: methodology, benefits, harms, applicability, and certainty.

Each of the 42 included trials, comprising 32 alcohol studies, 4 smoking studies, and 6 opioid studies, was assigned to either Tier 1 or Tier 2\. Tier 1 studies reported a statistic that could be mathematically converted into a standardized between-groups effect size, specifically Hedges’ g, using an established conversion formula and without requiring the calculation of a new statistical test not reported by the original authors. These 16 studies were placed on a common numeric scale and presented together in the forest plot, thereby allowing their effect magnitudes to be visually compared and, in principle, synthesized quantitatively. The reported results of Tier 2 studies could not be converted to a standardized effect size on this common scale due to the absence of a comparator arm, the absence of a reported test statistic, or the use of a statistic not reducible to a one-degree-of-freedom between-groups comparison. Rather than excluding these 26 studies from the review, we classified the direction and approximate magnitude of each effect on the basis of the information reported by the original authors, using categories such as negative, null, small positive, moderate positive, large positive, single-arm positive, or unclassifiable. Because these results were not expressed on a common poolable scale, they were displayed in a categorical plot rather than a forest plot.

For all Tier 1 studies, we attempted to convert each study’s reported inferential statistic into a standardized mean-difference effect size, beginning with Cohen’s d and subsequently applying the Hedges small-sample bias correction to obtain Hedges’ g. We did not compute new statistical tests from raw data when such tests were not reported by the original authors; instead, each conversion was based exclusively on a statistic provided in the source paper. The specific conversion rule depended on the type of statistic reported. When Cohen’s d or Hedges’ g was already reported, the value was used directly. When a study reported a one-way F statistic with one numerator degree of freedom, corresponding to a two-group comparison, we calculated d as 2 multiplied by the square root of F divided by the error degrees of freedom. When partial eta-squared was reported for a two-group comparison, we calculated d as 2 multiplied by the square root of eta-squared divided by one minus eta-squared. When a chi-square statistic with one degree of freedom was reported from a 2 × 2 group-by-outcome table, we first converted the statistic to phi by taking the square root of chi-square divided by total N, and then calculated d as 2 multiplied by phi divided by the square root of one minus phi-squared. When an odds ratio was reported, we applied the standard Hasselblad-Hedges logit-to-d conversion, calculating d as the natural logarithm of the odds ratio multiplied by the square root of 3 and divided by pi. When a risk ratio was reported, we applied the same log-based formula as an approximation, but only in cases where the outcome was relatively rare.

Each resulting d value was then bias-corrected to Hedges’ g using the correction factor J, such that g \= d × J, where J \= 1 − 3/(4df − 1\) and df \= total N − 2\. The sampling variance of g was estimated using the standard formula for a two-independent-groups design. When a study reported only the total sample size and did not provide separate arm sizes, we assumed equal group sizes (n1 \= n2 \= total N/2) for the purpose of estimating variance, because the required allocation information was otherwise unavailable. This simplifying assumption is noted in the figure legend. 

Of the 42 clinical trials, 16 reported a statistic reducible to a one-degree-of-freedom between-groups comparison and were carried forward to quantitative pooling. Each was converted to Hedges' g under a fixed precedence with the small-sample correction applied and the sampling variance computed on the same basis. Where a trial reported only a total sample size, equal group sizes were assumed for variance estimation. Conversions were graded clean or approximate according to whether the reported statistic mapped to g without additional distributional assumptions, and both grades were pooled. The 16 estimates were combined by inverse-variance weighting under a DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986, 2015), chosen over a fixed-effect model because the trials span three substance-use conditions, four psychedelic compounds, and six decades of clinical practice. Heterogeneity is reported as Cochran's Q, the between-study variance τ², and I², with a 95% prediction interval for the effect in a future trial. To place the pooled estimate on the same scale as the comparator interventions in Table 5, the pooled g was back-transformed to an odds ratio by the logistic approximation OR \= exp(g × π/√3). Robustness was assessed by leave-one-out deletion and by pooling the clean and approximate conversions separately.

### 3.2 Net benefits

Additionally, the study considered net benefits, a major consideration for USPSTF. Here, based upon our literature review, we included preliminary responses to the three central areas of inquiry addressed by the framework: 1\) Benefits: Do psychedelic-assisted interventions improve the behaviors that are known to cause mortality, morbidity, and other adverse health and social outcomes in adults who currently smoke, or have problematic use of alcohol or opioids? Do they provide co-benefits such as improved mental, physiological, or social health?  2\) Harms: Are adverse events or side effects associated with their use?  Here, we applied the definition of Adverse Events established in the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, V.5 (CTCAE; DHHS, 2017). 3\) Net benefits: do the benefits significantly outweigh the harms? A final assessment considered by the USPSTF, the equitable distribution of benefits, was not considered in this analysis, in part due to the homogeneity of the underlying data.  

### 3.3 Benchmarking

By drawing from USPSTF reports, we profiled the volume of evidence that formed the basis for a category A/B recommendation for a range of interventions that might prove analogous to psychedelics in terms of net benefits, including tobacco (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2021), cardiovascular disease (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2022), HIV/AIDS (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2019), alcohol (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2018), and opioid and other unhealthy drug use (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2020). For each, we catalogued the number of studies and participants, pooled effect sizes (with 95% confidence intervals, standardized as Hedges’ g statistics), and the USPSTF’s assessment of the certainty and magnitude of net benefit (high, moderate, or low, and substantial, moderate, small, or zero/negative, respectively). The USPSTF also accounts for the disease burden of the preventable condition under consideration when assessing evidence sufficiency. We profiled the disease burdens based upon standard considerations (DALYs, mortality) and differentiating characteristics (acuity of outcomes, societal impacts). The general body of psychedelic science was considered relative to these examples to posit which intervention’s volume of evidence could serve as a target or benchmark for a USPSTF review of psychedelic science.

# Results

1. ## Methodological Evaluation

   The literature search identified 75 peer-reviewed articles of psychedelics: 42 eligible clinical-trial articles (32 alcohol, 6 opioid, 4 smoking), and 33 observational studies. Every observational study was assignable to at least one review condition (19 alcohol, 12 opioid, 5 tobacco), with three studies contributing to more than one condition (Anderson 2019, alcohol and tobacco; Thomas 2013, alcohol, opioid, and tobacco); see Table 2\. These classifications indicate that, among clinical trials in particular, specific drugs were relatively condition-bound. For smoking, 100% of trials used psilocybin. For alcohol trials, 38% used LSD, 25% psilocybin, another 25% used ketamine, and 12% used MDMA. For opioid trials, 50% used ibogaine, 33% used ketamine, and 17% used LSD. No trial included ayahuasca, though ten observational studies did. One alcohol trial (Smith 1958\) administered both LSD and mescaline, and is the sole trial in the sample using mescaline or more than one psychedelic.

   Because USPSTF prioritizes clinical trials, the analyses focused its methodological assessment on the 42 clinical trial publications (Supplemental Table S.1-Table of all included studies). Table 3 details the indicators that address USPSTF methodological considerations, organized across five domains, as follows:

   ***Study Identification & Design*** Across all 6 domains, no study met all criteria. 60% of trials involved randomization of participants to an active arm or a comparator, and was higher in opioid (83%) and alcohol (59%) trials than in tobacco trials (25%). Blinding of any form was reported in 50% of trials; whereas 67% of opioid trials utilized blinding, no tobacco studies did (0%). Similarly, double-blinding was used in 50% of opioid trials, and was absent in tobacco studies. A caveat is that successful blinding of psychedelic studies is notoriously difficult, and functional unblinding rates are typically high (van Elk and Fried 2023).

   While 76% of all trials reported using validated outcome measurement scales, 100% of tobacco studies did so compared to 72% for alcohol and 83% for opioids.Twenty four percent of the total sample reported results of power calculations. Importantly, only one (2%) of all trials included an interface with primary care settings (Grabski, 2022), which is required for a USPSTF recommendation.

   ***Population & Generalizability*** Baseline severity was reported in 98% of trials overall, 97% alcohol; 100% opioid; 100% tobacco. Female representation averaged 29% overall (alcohol 31%; opioids 15%; tobacco 35%), while BIPOC representation was highest in opioid trials (51%) compared to alcohol (20%) and tobacco (8%). Only 2% of trials recruited a participant pool reflective of real-world community or primary care populations, and no opioid or tobacco trial did so. Inclusion of low-SES participants was limited (19% overall). Fewer than half of trials (48%) were conducted in the United States, and only one of six opioid trials (17%) was, further limiting applicability to US primary care. 

   ***Intervention and Safety*** All trials included description of the intervention, which involved therapeutic support in 100% of tobacco, 88% alcohol and 50% of opioid studies. Overall, 86% of trials provided a summary of adverse events (100% tobacco; 100% of opioid; 81% of alcohol studies).

   ***Equity & Cultural Framing*** No study referenced Indigenous frameworks or addressed reciprocity for Indigenous communities (0% for both). A single trial (Savage 1973, 2% of the sample) employed an explicit cultural or spiritual frame. See also the Population & Generalizability indicators, which suggest to-date clinical trials have not robustly addressed equity considerations.

   ***Outcomes & Follow-up*** Complete cessation was reported in 71% of studies, including 100% of tobacco studies. Relapse was tracked in 83% of opioid trials and 75% in tobacco, but only 53% of alcohol studies. 100% of tobacco and opioid studies measured physical/biological outcomes, compared to 56% of alcohol studies. Measurement of implementation outcomes (29%), quality of life (14%) and mortality (12%) remained low across the entire sample.

## 

2. ## Net benefits

   The USPSTF makes its assessment in terms of net benefits and net magnitude, weighing risks against gains. Figures 2A and B illustrate that the effect sizes (benefits) of psychedelic-interventions to-date are consistent, large, and positive.  Among the 42 trials totalling 2,098 participants, the majority (81%) reported improvement in problematic substance use (tobacco: 100%; opioids: 83%; alcohol: 78%), with a pooled effect size of 2.30 (1.49 \- 3.55).  Thirty seven (86%) trials reported assessing AEs, and among these, 12 (28%) recorded at least one moderate/severe adverse event. Across the 36 trials reporting AEs,185 discrete AEs were recorded, of which 144 (78%) were mild and 24 (13%) severe. The 33 observational studies totaled approximately 979,474 participants (58,078 excluding Jones et al. 2022a, 2022b, and 2025); 85% (28/33) report positive effects. Among the observational studies, 67% (22) reported assessing AEs, with 11 (50%) of these recording at least one moderate/severe AE. Among 103 AEs recorded, 75 were mild, (75%), while 11% were severe. The percentage of AEs relative to total N is lower among observational studies, but the distribution of mild, moderate, severe AEs between these trials is quite similar (Table 4). Looking at the general population participating in the Oregon state psilocybin program, Korthuis et al. (2026) found an even lower level of severe AEs, with 1.2%, of study participants experiencing adverse behavioral reactions requiring medical attention.

3. ## Benchmarking

   The USPSTF is guided by methodological standards held in common across interventions. However, the volume of evidence informing USPSTF recommendations, such as the number of studies and participants, varies by intervention because the USPSTF evaluates the certainty and magnitude of net benefit rather than only applying a fixed evidentiary threshold based on volume (Barry, 2023). To explore the dynamic between research volume, effects, and net benefit, Table 5 compares several pharmaceutical or substance-use interventions that received a Category A or B rating from the USPSTF to roughly benchmark to a profile that might receive a similar recommendation for preventive psychedelics.  

   The profile of effects across the 16 included trials contributing a convertible effect estimate (N \= 973), shows the pooled random-effects standardized mean difference was g \= 0.46 (95% CI 0.22–0.70; z \= 3.78, p \< 0.001), equivalent to an odds ratio of 2.30 (1.49–3.55). Heterogeneity was substantial (Q \= 46.1 on 15 df, p \< 0.001; τ² \= 0.146; I² \= 67%), and the 95% prediction interval for a future trial spans −0.33 to 1.25. The estimate is nonetheless stable to the removal of any single trial, with leave-one-out pooling ranging from g \= 0.42 (omitting Johnson MW 2026\) to g \= 0.53 (omitting Hollister 1969). At g \= 0.46 the psychedelic estimate exceeds the statin (0.047–0.228), alcohol screening and brief intervention (0.293), and opioid screening (0.262) benchmarks, and lies closest to HIV PrEP (0.427). In a few key instances, such as for Varenicline and HIVPrEP, we see relatively smaller total studies and N along with larger effects, potentially pointing toward a benchmark for preventive psychedelic science. 

    HIV PrEP might be the most suitable possible benchmark for psychedelic interventions due to similarities in terms of large observed effect sizes, as well as other considerations such as high near-term risks for serious negative health outcomes and large societal burdens in the absence of preventive measures, and surrounding stigma. With a smaller number of studies and total participants, a PrEP benchmark is also more attainable in a shorter timespan.

   # Discussion

   Employing a public health prevention lens and “policy backward” framework, this study evaluated the developments needed to produce a forward-facing research roadmap capable of establishing psychedelic interventions as a preventive measure suitable for primary care settings and generating a USPSTF nomination and Category A/B recommendation. Finding that no study examined in this sample met all USPSTF-aligned indicators underscores the current gap between experimental research and the evidentiary standards required for preventive service recommendations by the USPSTF. 

   Even so, there is promising alignment with the USPSTF net benefit framework and an attainable evidentiary benchmark. In other words, these findings suggest that it is feasible to build a body of evidence that, with reliable certainty, meets the standards required by the USPSTF. So far, the effect sizes of psychedelic-intervention are consistently large and positive. Of 185 recorded adverse events across the 42 trials, 78% graded mild and just 13% (24) graded severe adverse (less than 2% per \~2000 participants). The literature supports this net benefit profile, finding that, regardless of clinical intent, psychedelic interventions (classic psychedelics in particular) are relatively safe in controlled settings, with infrequent, and usually mild-to-moderate adverse events (Hinkle, 2024; Yerubandi, 2024; Freitus, 2025). 

   This study elucidates research priorities to bridge the evidentiary gap between treatment and prevention. In particular, investment should emphasize research that addresses external validity and implementation settings. The trials in this study did not adequately reflect the populations and settings where preventive services are usually delivered. Only 2% of clinical trials recruited participants representative of real-world community or primary care populations, only 19% included low socioeconomic status (SES) participants, average female participation was 29%, average BIPOC participation was 21%, and only 2% of studies involved primary care. 

   These gaps are not surprising since early psychedelic clinical trials focused on safety and efficacy, with limited consideration of both acute psychedelic drug effects on an individual basis, and their scaling to population levels (DellaCrosse et al., 2024). And yet, without population and setting representation, policy and practice bodies cannot make critical decisions regarding access, delivery models, costs, reimbursements, etc. Here we have focused on the USPSTF, but a similar call was recently made in the report, *Psychedelic-Assisted Therapy and Medicaid: Considerations for Coverage and Access*. It recommended that investment in research align with state Medicaid coverage and service provision considerations, in particular reflecting Medicaid populations, addressing setting and staffing parameters, and generating data aligned with Medicaid stakeholder interests (CHCS, 2026).

   Other gaps among the trials included the small sample sizes, narrow target populations, and functional unblinding. However, a number of phase 2-3 clinical trials are underway in large, heterogeneous populations ([ClinicalTrials.gov](http://ClinicalTrials.gov) 2026 a/b), and methodological limitations are receiving attention from government funders (NIH RFA-MH-27-135). This growing investment in larger, better-powered, and more rigorously designed trials suggests that many of the evidentiary gaps identified here are addressable. Supplementing evidence from these trials with large observational studies can help identify downstream impacts on prevention targets.

   Equity considerations are increasingly emphasized by USPSTF, signalling that they should similarly rise in importance in psychedelic research design. This is another case for investment in participant pools more reflective of the general, or primary care, population. Cultural framing and reciprocity for Indigenous communities could be included as they represent best public health practice, and represent a step toward reciprocity, given Western psychedelic science is built upon Indigenous expertise and stewardship of sacred plant medicines. 

   ## Limitations

   There are several limitations of this study. The first pertains to the incompleteness of the methodological indicators and the focus on individual studies. An actual USPSTF review would be more comprehensive, grapple with a dynamic comparison of different studies, and emphasize pooled/meta/summary studies. Furthermore, the AI-based extraction process may have led to errors and misinterpretation of codes, although this possibility was mitigated by conducting a coding second pass and having human reviewers verify each final cell. In terms of benchmarking to other USPSTF-recommended interventions, given the heterogeneity and small number of contributing trials, and the fact that five of the 16 estimates rest on approximate conversions, this comparison is directional rather than a defensible meta-analytic summary. 

   Even so, the present study provides sufficient proof-of-concept to demonstrate the relevance of a psychedelic prevention framework and point toward priority design areas for psychedelic science. The staggering personal and population health and social burdens of problematic substance use, and the large effect sizes and population health potential seen in psychedelic research to-date, give merit to a research roadmap. That roadmap should establish the efficacy of psychedelic interventions as preventive of associated preclinical health changes and adverse health and socioeconomic outcomes. This approach mirrors the Grade A tobacco cessation precedent, where cessation in current smokers is treated as prevention against downstream chronic diseases (USPSTF, 2021a). 

   A starting point is to invest in research design that incorporates the evidentiary standards of the USPSTF, especially concerning participant profile and applicability to the primary care context. To support prevention claims, psychedelic science should also extend follow-up windows to capture change in morbidity and mortality outcomes associated with problematic substance use. Those follow-up windows could also be mapped to typical relapse milestones to profile optimal continuity of care for the prevention of adverse health outcomes. To design for policy, behavior change effect sizes could be modelled onto established disease trajectories to estimate averted adverse outcomes and associated costs. In general, designing psychedelic studies that address payer concerns regarding economic endpoints should be considered fundamental. 

   In addition to supporting expansion of the conceptual frame to incorporate preventive care, this assessment highlights two important directions that psychedelic science can advance for expanded access. 

   ## 1\. Primary care compatibility 

   The USPSTF specifically addresses prevention within a primary care context in terms of service delivery and populations served. Psychedelic-assisted therapy has been developed almost exclusively within psychiatry or mental health service models, but this may not be the optimal, or most equitable, home for it at scale. Primary care lowers costs, and has a track record of prevention as well as treatment. Further, primary care providers already shoulder a substantial proportion of mental health care in the US, filling gaps created by psychiatric workforce shortages and insurance barriers. These considerations point to the importance of investigating psychedelic interventions within the context of  primary care.

   Several features of psychedelic interventions specifically favor a primary care model. These compounds can produce significant acute physiologic effects, including elevations in blood pressure and heart rate, that call for clinical monitoring and risk stratification. Primary care clinicians, who routinely assess cardiovascular risk, are well-positioned to conduct pre-treatment screening and provide medical oversight during sessions. At the same time, frequent col-location of services in the primary care setting lend themselves to the therapy components of psychedelic treatment that do not require a physician. The preparation, session support, and integration work that drive therapeutic outcomes are well within the scope of co-located behavioral health providers such as social workers and marriage and family therapists, community health workers, non-clinical state-certified facilitators, and even peer support specialists.

   A collaborative care model, in which a primary care physician provides medical oversight and a non-physician provider conducts the therapeutic work, is not only clinically coherent but economically compelling. Such a collaborative approach is well-established within primary care, closely aligning with the Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment (SBIRT) framework, and is already under consideration by the USPSTF for unhealthy alcohol use in adults and adolescents (USPSTF, 2025b). In this existing model, primary care physicians oversee screening and medical stratification, while co-located behavioral health clinicians provide the counseling and facilitate necessary care transitions. Psychedelic-assisted interventions could utilize a parallel workflow, where primary care physicians manage pre-treatment assessments and safety monitoring, leaving the preparation, session facilitation, and therapeutic integration to behavioral health specialists or other trained facilitators and preparation/integration providers. This structure allows the physician to serve in a supervisory and on-call capacity while containing costs and expanding capacity and access. Studies should test models in which medical screening and oversight are provided by primary care physicians and therapeutic support is provided by non-physician providers. Family medicine and general internal medicine departments should actively support faculty research in psychedelic medicine.

   There is also a representational argument. Primary care practices and co-located behavioral health teams tend to reflect the demographics of the communities they serve more closely, and also are present in tribal communities. Delivering psychedelic therapy through these settings could improve cultural competence, reduce therapeutic mistrust, and generate efficacy data in more diverse and generalizable populations.

   ## 2\. Expanding consideration to include observational studies, state-regulated programs, other registries 

   There is merit in increasing the stature of alternative research designs and data sources for USPSTF deliberations and other policy and coverage decisions. State psychedelic programs and other registries, platform studies as trial alternatives, and large, well-designed observational studies, especially with prospective designs, all can achieve large and diverse study populations. Another significant benefit is their potential to monitor adverse events / risks on a mass scale. For example, a recent study of the first year of Oregon Psilocybin Services operations, found that adverse events \- behavioral or medical \- requiring facilitator intervention beyond normal support, medical provider contact, or emergency services were rare, with annual rates of 2.42 and 2.79 per 1,000 sessions, respectively (Yu, 2026). According to OHA’s Q12026 records, as of June 2026, total adverse events, including post-session, are recorded in 0.33% of more than 22,000 people served, and only 32 (0.15%) sessions involved calls to emergency services. 

   From a public health perspective, observational studies are more reflective of the settings where the significant majority of psychedelics will be consumed, regardless of their regulatory status. In fact, far more people have had exposure to psychedelics than is common for novel compounds seeking regulatory approval; an estimated 11 million US adults took psilocybin in the past year alone (RAND, 2025). In the case of psychedelics, observational and registry data sets may be well-suited to meet USPSTF criteria for net benefits, net magnitude, external validity and equity. Further, as illustrated in Table 4, above, there are no drug interventions recommended by USPSTF for prevention of AUD or OUD, indicating high unmet need, especially given the urgency of the opioid crisis and the high portion of current smokers who want to quit (Babb, 2017), making these data sources even more salient.

   State psychedelic program data also represent a significant opportunity to accelerate development of the evidence base needed for USPSTF approval. While Schedule I status restricts commercial distribution and prescribing, it does not preclude systematic evaluation, surveillance, or public health monitoring of state-legal activities. The nascent regulatory structures in Oregon, Colorado, and other states therefore offer a critical policy opportunity to establish comprehensive, real-world surveillance and evaluation systems that provide the scale of data the field requires and the USPSTF needs for its determinations. 

   For example, although Oregon Psilocybin Services (OPS) is designed as a non-medical wellness model requiring no diagnosis (Yu, 2026), a substantial portion of participants report motivations that align with conditions managed in psychiatry and primary care, such as anxiety, depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders (Yu, 2026). Consequently, a significant share of this "non-medical" population is *de facto* treatment-seeking. This presents an opportunity to track safety and estimate net benefits, if these systems monitor changes in behaviors that can prevent adverse health outcomes under real-world conditions. The ORCHID project (Oregon-Colorado Regulated Psychedelic Care: Healthcare Impacts & Decisions), is an example that aims to link state-regulated psilocybin services to changes in healthcare costs, utilization, and health outcomes. 

   Capitalizing on this opportunity necessitates ensuring that state-licensed service centers capture key prevention and health promotion measures, including mental health trajectories, substance use and other behavioral or lifestyle patterns, the associated health outcomes, and healthcare utilization. These metrics should be standardized, compatible with existing state health priorities and metrics such as reflected in State Health Improvement Plans (SHIPs), and link to county-level data. Such integration would scale the psychedelic evidence base through the broader prevention and population health monitoring architecture. State- academic partnerships could ensure the evidentiary standards for prevention are met, standardize outcome measurement, and extend follow-up beyond the acute session, generating insights on net benefits and prevention through longitudinal, real-world safety and effectiveness data that surpass current clinical trials and aggregate state dashboards. States that implement credible monitoring systems are also better positioned to advocate for expanded coverage and reimbursement through Medicaid waivers, state employee health plans, or private insurer negotiations. 

   # Conclusion and Path Forward

   To our knowledge, this study is the first public health-informed review aimed at outlining a research roadmap to expand psychedelic care access through preventive services. Just as the feasibility of integrating psychedelic care into substance use disorder treatment models has been positively assessed (Yaden, 2024), so too can it be considered for primary care-based preventive care. 

   To do so will involve prioritization and investment that enables overcoming or circumventing the limitations and internal validity threats frequently encountered in psychedelic trials (Weleff, 2025). It also requires that research and investment place greater emphasis on external validity, follow-up duration, primary care settings, and interventions targeted at earlier points in the progression of substance use and health outcome trajectories. Leadership that incorporates and prioritizes prevention’s evidentiary standards in psychedelic science could produce significant gains. The opportunity to subsequently generate a shared research agenda and common evidentiary standards that bridge treatment and preventive models and heighten roles for methodologies such as prospective meta analysis and platform trials is valuable. If coordinated globally, a funded research agenda prioritizing preventive care could more rapidly scale psychedelic interventions from clinical breakthroughs to expanded preventive services for improved access and population health.
